title: A temporary public job can keep some marginal workers attached to employment for years
source_unit: SEHSD-WP2026-05 using 2010 Decennial Applicant, Personnel, and Payroll System records linked to Census demographic records and 2005-2023 IRS Form W-2 records
geography: United States; applicants for temporary 2010 Decennial Census jobs and linked employment outcomes

observations.period: 2010 Census hiring; W-2 outcomes observed through 2023; paper published March 2026

denominator.unit: rounded applicants who appeared on at least one Census selection sheet; estimates focus on non-veteran applicants and score-defined comparison groups

scale.value: The 2010 Decennial Census recruited about 3.9 million applicants for more than 850,000 temporary positions; about 2.3 million applicants appeared on at least one selection sheet

marginal_2010_employment.value: For applicants just around the generally required score of 70, receiving a Census job was associated with a 61 percentage-point increase in the likelihood of W-2 employment in 2010

marginal_2023_employment.value: For the same marginal score group, Census hires were 28 percentage points more likely to receive a W-2 in 2023 than comparable applicants not hired

wages.value: Conditional on working, post-2010 W-2 wages did not differ significantly; the higher likelihood of working translated to nearly $6,000 more annual W-2 wages for marginal hires
wages.unit: conditional wage and total annual W-2 outcome

heterogeneity_and_cost.value: The long-run employment effect for marginal applicants was concentrated among men, while low-score Census workers were more than twice as likely to be terminated for misconduct or unsatisfactory performance as higher-score workers

average_applicant_effect.value: Across the broader test-score distribution, hiring increased the likelihood of W-2 employment by about 22 percentage points in 2010 but the effect dissipated by 2011
average_applicant_effect.unit: short-run employment estimate for broader applicant group

observations.method: The study uses a fuzzy regression-discontinuity design around the generally required employment-test score of 70 for marginal applicants and a within-selection-sheet comparison for broader applicants. It links restricted hiring records to Census demographic records and IRS W-2 outcomes from 2005 through 2023.
observations.uncertainty: This is a Census SEHSD working paper and not a Census Bureau endorsement. The local discontinuity estimate applies to applicants near the score threshold, not all unemployed people or all public jobs. The 2010 Census setting included a large recession-era labor market, a background check, training, trust-sensitive enumeration work, and a particular selection process; the study cannot show that the same effects would occur under a different public hiring design or stronger labor market.
observations.subgroup: Non-veteran temporary Census applicants, with comparisons by test score, sex, age, education, race/ethnicity, Medicaid/SNAP exposure, and urbanicity; long-run marginal-applicant effects were concentrated among men.
observations.counterinterpretation: The job itself may help through income, work attachment, a résumé signal, passing a background check, training, or the specific trust requirements of Census work. Hiring may also displace private work for applicants who would otherwise have worked; the broader applicant effect fades quickly. Termination, management time, replacement, and work-quality costs are only partly observed, and W-2 employment is not job quality, wellbeing, or household security.

boundary: This record adds a bounded public-hiring-to-labor-attachment pathway. It does not establish a universal job-guarantee effect, a national employment rate, equal benefit across groups, job quality, household wellbeing, or political legitimacy.
